extracted.intended_audience: researchers and practitioners in physics-informed machine learning, computational scientists and applied mathematicians developing/assessing PINNs, DeepONets and related ML models for PDEs and physical systems
extracted.subtask_description: Designing, training, evaluating and analysing physics-informed machine learning models (e.g., PINNs, DeepONets) for forward/inverse PDE problems, multiphysics and multiscale applications with attention to architecture, losses, training, uncertainty and theoretical guarantees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training algorithm and sample-size selection
rubrics_metrics.description: Which training algorithm to choose? How many training samples to consider? There are currently no rule-of-thumb strategies and experience is required to set up a physics-informed ML model properly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choices intimately depend on the specific task. Emerging meta-learning techniques could automate architecture and algorithm selection. Consider transfer learning and scalable/parallel training (GPUs/TPUs, data- and model-parallelism) to reduce cost. No a priori guarantee for required sample complexity — iterative/empirical selection is often necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architecture choice matched to problem and data modality
rubrics_metrics.description: The underlying architecture of a PINNs model is determined by the nature of a given problem: multi-layer perceptron architectures are generally applicable but do not encode specialized inductive biases; convolutional NNs are suitable for gridded 2D domains; Fourier feature networks are suitable for PDEs whose solution exhibits high frequencies or periodic boundaries; recurrent architectures are suitable for non-Markovian and time-discrete problems. DeepONet can be used to infer an operator (instead of a function).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select architectures based on data type (scattered sensor measurements → MLP, images → CNN, time series → RNN) and desired inductive biases. Be mindful that architecture may need to change with varying system parameters (e.g., bifurcation parameters). Empirical design is common but expensive; meta-learning can help automate search.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of probabilistic variants for uncertainty quantification
rubrics_metrics.description: Probabilistic variants of PINNs can be used to infer stochastic processes that capture epistemic/model uncertainty (via Bayesian inference or frequentist ensembles) or aleatoric uncertainty (via generative models such as variational auto-encoders and GANs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate Bayesian methods, ensembles, or generative-model approaches when uncertainty estimates are important for downstream tasks (e.g., digital twins, forecasts). Choice of probabilistic model affects training complexity and required data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sample complexity determinants
rubrics_metrics.description: Required sample complexity is typically not known a priori and is generally determined by: the strength of inductive biases used in the architecture; the compatibility between the observed data and the underlying physical law used as regularization; and the complexity of the underlying function or operator to be approximated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate needed samples by considering model bias, physics-compatibility, and target complexity. Use stronger inductive biases or operator-learning frameworks to reduce sample needs when possible. Expect task-specific variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiscale and high-frequency components (spectral bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fully connected NNs have difficulty learning high-frequency functions (the 'F-principle' or 'spectral bias'); high-frequency features cause steep gradients making it hard to accurately penalize PDE residuals, leading to training failure for multiscale problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation techniques include domain decomposition, Fourier feature embeddings, multiscale DNN architectures, phase-shift networks, and other methods specifically designed to capture high-frequency content. Consider hp-refinement and problem-specific representations to aid learning of oscillatory components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling multiphysics coupling
rubrics_metrics.description: Learning multiphysics simultaneously can be computationally expensive and networks may struggle; one strategy is to learn each physics separately and then couple them together (e.g., DeepM&M with several DeepONets trained per field and then coupled).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multiphysics problems, consider decomposing into subproblems, training specialized operator surrogates, and composing/coupling them (parallel or serial architectures). Use additional supervised data where needed to learn coupling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Loss function formulation and limitations of point-wise losses
rubrics_metrics.description: Currently in NN-based ML methods, physics-informed loss functions are mainly defined in a point-wise way; such loss functions can fail in some low-dimensional cases (for example diffusion equation with non-smooth conductivity/permeability).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explore alternative loss formulations (weak/variational forms, quadrature-based losses, continuous-loss formulations). Use hp-refinement, quadrature point selection, or variational PINNs to improve approximation and generalization in problematic cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training stability, competing loss terms, and optimization pathologies
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics-informed ML models often involve large-scale NNs with complicated loss functions that consist of multiple terms and are highly non-convex; terms in the loss may compete during training causing instability and lack of convergence to global minima. Spectral bias can induce discrepancies in convergence rates of different loss components and vanishing back-propagated gradients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design robust NN architectures and training algorithms (e.g., use weak-form losses, hp-refinement via decomposition, adaptive activation modification, adaptive sampling of residual/evaluation points). Mitigate imbalance among loss terms (reweighting, multi-objective strategies). Use insights from NTK or optimization theory to inform training.

rubrics_metrics.name: Architectural and algorithmic automation (meta-learning) and transfer learning
rubrics_metrics.description: Design of effective NN architectures is currently done empirically by users and can be time-consuming; emerging meta-learning techniques can be used to automate architecture and hyperparameter search. Transfer learning (e.g., via DeepONets) can speed up learning across related tasks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt meta-learning or architecture search to reduce manual tuning; use transfer learning across parameter regimes or similar tasks to accelerate convergence and reduce required data/training time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Efficient computation of higher-order, integral and fractional derivatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Physics-informed ML usually involves higher-order derivatives; their efficient evaluation is not well supported in popular frameworks (TensorFlow, PyTorch). Other operators such as integral operators and fractional-order derivatives are also useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop or use ML libraries that support efficient higher-order derivative computation (e.g., Taylor-mode automatic differentiation) and fractional/integral operators to lower computational cost. Consider algorithmic and software choices that reduce cost of derivative evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Benchmarks, datasets, curation and evaluation metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: The ML community uses standard benchmarks to assess algorithmic improvement, reproducibility and computational cost; physics-informed ML needs curated, public datasets (including full-field simulation data where experiments cannot provide it) and meaningful benchmarks that test accuracy and speed-up, including hardware/software considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully curate and publish datasets with accompanying physical models and generation parameters. Design benchmarks that probe dynamical prediction, bifurcation detection, and chaotic states. Consider new metrics such as 'valid-time-prediction' for dynamical forecasting. Account for compute/hardware in evaluations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical foundations: error decomposition, well-posedness, stability and convergence
rubrics_metrics.description: A new theory is required to analyse the capabilities and limitations of constrained NNs: can a network find solutions to PDEs via gradient-based optimization? Total error should be decomposed into approximation error, optimization error and generalization error; well-posedness, stability and convergence should be analysed, particularly when operators are learned from data and initial/boundary conditions are uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop rigorous analyses quantifying approximation capacity, optimization dynamics, and statistical generalization. Use compactness, norm equivalences, and complexity measures to obtain sufficient conditions for convergence. Address well-posedness when learned operators are involved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularization and generalization analysis techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques cited include Hölder regularization to control derivatives of neural networks and bound generalization error, rademacher complexity to handle sample-based generalization, quadrature-based formulations for abstract error estimates, and neural tangent kernel (NTK) perspectives for training dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply appropriate regularization (e.g., Hölder-type) and complexity-control methods to bound generalization. Use quadrature and continuous-loss error-estimate frameworks, Rademacher complexity bounds for sample-based analyses, and NTK/overparameterization theory to understand convergence regimes. These methods complement empirical evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visualization of loss landscapes and equivalence analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding training by visualizing the landscape of loss functions for different formulations (strong form, weak form, etc.) is helpful. It is important to understand equivalence between models and between different loss functions with different norms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use loss-landscape visualization and comparative analyses to diagnose optimization issues and to assess when alternative formulations are effectively equivalent. This can guide selection between strong/weak/variational approaches and inform reparameterizations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learning intrinsic variables, emergent representations and latent-space geometry
rubrics_metrics.description: An emerging paradigm is to use observations and learning methods to automatically determine intrinsic variables and useful physical model formulations. Manifold learning techniques (ISOMAP, t-SNE, diffusion maps) and deep generative/variational autoencoders embed observations into reduced latent spaces where evolution rules/operators can be learned; emergent 'space-times' and ML-driven independent variables are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use manifold learning/autoencoder approaches to discover compact, informative latent variables. Integrate active learning to select informative experiments guided by latent-space geometry. Expect these representations to aid model discovery, reduced-order modelling and design optimization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data/model transformations, fusion and interpretability
rubrics_metrics.description: Different researchers may produce different data-driven models for the same phenomenon; building ML-based transformations between predictive models, models at different fidelities, and theories that are transformable/calibratable to each other is important for fusion and interpretability. Transformations between ML latent-space features and physically interpretable observables (or ML-learned operators and closed-form equations) bolster interpretability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop mappings between ML models and physical models, test transformation validity and generalization limits (for which observations models can be mapped). Use these transformations to fuse models of differing fidelity and to increase interpretability and calibration capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tooling, visualization environments and user-friendly development platforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Extended requirements for physical problems include incorporating multiple physics and complicated geometry domains into the learning algorithm, and visualizing the solution field (even high-dimensional ones) similar to platforms like FEniCS or OpenFOAM. A user-friendly, graph-based ML development environment could help practitioners develop physics-informed ML algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invest in tooling that supports complex geometries, multi-physics setups, high-dimensional visualization, model graph inspection, metric tracking and reproducible experiments. Such environments lower the barrier for domain specialists to adopt physics-informed ML.

rubrics_metrics.name: Digital-twin readiness: heterogeneous data, preprocessing/calibration and real-time constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: For digital twins, observational data can be scarce, noisy and heterogeneous (images, time series, lab tests, clinical records) and may not directly contain quantities of interest; physics-based models require costly preprocessing and calibration (mesh generation, boundary/initial condition calibration), hampering real-time decision-making.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design methods that can assimilate heterogeneous, scarce/noisy data, reduce preprocessing overhead (automatic differentiation can remove mesh needs), and enable rapid calibration. Address constraints for real-time decision-making by improving computational efficiency and robustness.
